title: DWP 'cyber incident' causes millions to lose access to benefits and pensions services
description: Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cybe
body: Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.The UK's former Chief Technology Officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the incident was an attack."They've taken down some of the citizen-facing services which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door," he said.Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC the technological disruption meant she was missing £1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday."I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment."I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site."With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.As of around 12:00 GMT on Friday, the online systems for pensions, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died, could not be accessed.It was not clear when the government expected services to be up and running again.A DWP spokesperson said: "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption."A statement continued: "As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links."Tech disruption to major service around the world have hit the headlines repeatedly in recent months.There was a major outage of Microsoft services, the grounding of all US flights, problems at the US National Security Agency, and disruption at major American banks.The causes of these incidents have varied. Many were linked to upgrades going wrong but experts have also mentioned factors including outdated IT systems and the use of AI to potentially exploit tech vulnerabilities. While the nature of the DWP incident is unclear, officials could not rule out the involvement of a "malicious actor", but added there was "no evidence" that other government departments had been targeted in this way. The DWP outage follows warnings that AI technology could fuel attacks on UK digital infrastructure.Earlier this month a National Cyber Security Centre report urged organisations to strengthen their defences against hackers as the technology becomes more complex and capable. Its CEO Richard Horne said there was a "real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents".Last month the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a programming language used around the world.The PHP security flaw prompted a global race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.UK government websites have been impacted by other cyber incidents in recent years.In April 2025, the government reported that cyber attackers had breached the Legal Aid Agency's online services. It said the group responsible accessed a "significant amount" of personal data going back decades, including contact details of people who had applied for legal aid. The agency took some services offline while responding to the incident.

schema.headline: DWP 'cyber incident' causes millions to lose access to benefits and pensions services

title: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
description: Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she h
body: Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit."My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey."The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste"."I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink"."But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm"."It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011."They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks."I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry."I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'

title: Cold, flu and Covid symptoms: Expert advice and how to avoid the worst
description: Is it a cold, flu or Covid? How to tell the differenceImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 27 November 2026 09:43 GMTThere are lots of coughs and sneezes
body: Is it a cold, flu or Covid? How to tell the differenceImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 27 November 2026 09:43 GMTThere are lots of coughs and sneezes doing the rounds at the moment, so how do you know if it might be covid or flu rather than a cold?Here's how to spot the difference and hopefully avoid the worst this winter.What is flu?NHS leaders are already warning that the UK is seeing a "horrible spike" in flu, with hospital cases higher than usual for the time of year.Flu has hit a bit earlier than normal. And we are seeing a 'drifted' strain, external, say experts, meaning one that is slightly different to what was anticipated when this year's vaccine was being made.But vaccines still work against the virus that is constantly changing or mutating, they say. The vaccines are updated each year to ensure they continue to be a good match. So far this season, there's a mix of two flu A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2, circulating in England, says the UKHSA, external.The flu vaccine is designed to protect against all three main types of flu - influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and influenza B. Whichever ends up dominating this winter, or if they all circulate at similar levels throughout, the vaccine should offer broad protection.Some people can get a free NHS flu vaccine, external. Anyone else who wants one can buy it at a pharmacy.Flu symptoms tend to start more suddenly than a cold or Covid, and are usually more severe.Common flu symptoms include a fever, aching muscles and chills.Image source, Getty ImagesIs it a cold? Does cold weather cause it?Cold symptoms tend to be milder and come on more gradually than Covid or flu.It might include a sore throat, as well as coughing and sneezing.Research on the extent to which cold weather impacts our immune systems remains unclear.But darker days mean we typically make a beeline for warm, cosy, indoor spaces.And this environment is perfect for viruses.Schools, nursery and even some workplaces can be like a petri dish with lots of viruses circulating. The Christmas season raises the risks as more people socialise indoors. The same applies to freshers in university halls - where mixing together spreads germs, while heavy drinking and partying further weaken the immune system.Could it be Covid?Image source, Getty ImagesIt is still possible to catch Covid. Common symptoms include a high temperature and a cough, as well as feeling exhausted. One key Covid-specific identifier can be a loss of smell or taste. While no one is told to isolate any more, the advice is try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people if you or your child have symptoms.Most people do not need to take a Covid test if they have symptoms, but they are available to buy in chemists and, while not 100% accurate, they can help confirm or rule out infection.ColdsSymptoms appear graduallyMostly affect nose and throatEarly sign - pressure in your earsChestier, mucus coughFluComes on suddenlyFeel wiped outFever, muscle aches, exhaustionNeed bed restDry coughCovidTypical flu symptomsLoss of taste or smellDiarrhoea or tummy upsetMany of the symptoms between cold, flu and Covid, overlap.But there are some clues that might help you identify the exact culprit.If a cold's coming on, then it often does so gradually. It's going to affect your nose and the back of your throat, while some will get a tickling at the back of the mouth.Another early warning sign can be a build-up of pressure in the ear. If the virus spreads further, it can reach your lungs and cause a pesky cough.Mostly however, these symptoms don't stop us from carrying on as normal.The same can't be said for flu, which typically adds aches, fevers and muscle weakness into the mix. Flu doesn't always mean you have to go to bed, but it might make you feel that way.Since the pandemic, Covid has complicated things further, with similar symptoms to flu.The recommendation is to stay home and rest and recover. However, if you have underlying conditions, experience breathlessness or find symptoms don't ease after three weeks, then you shouldn't hesitate to seek medical advice.Can I help make myself better? Image source, Getty ImagesOur bodies naturally fight viruses and infection, but we can also give it a helping hand with the right medication. Paracetamol: Provided you're okay to take it, this or ibuprofen is the first port of call. Both are really good for helping to bring the fever down and softening any pain that you might have. But remember that lots of cough and cold mixtures include traces of paracetamol, so make sure you're not accidentally taking too muchVitamin C:  This is often thought to help defend against colds. But there's not a huge amount of evidence for this. Unless you're deficient, focusing on a healthy, balanced diet is far more importantVitamin D: A top-up of vitamin D in colder months is recommended by the NHS, because let's face it, we don't usually get much sunlight at this time of year in the UKDecongestant spray: Sure, they feel great and provide instant relief, but using sprays too often can cause rebound congestion- when your nose becomes dependent and swells without a fix. I suggest using them for no more than four of five daysChicken soup: There's little evidence of the dish fighting viruses directly, but its heat can help warm the back of your throat and soothe some of those symptoms. It's also a good way to take on extra fluids, with hydration vital as you battle infection.

schema.headline: Cold, flu and Covid symptoms: Expert advice and how to avoid the worst

title: Satellite imagery shows how fast Lagos and Alexandria are sinking
description: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinkingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be
body: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinkingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be exposed to extreme sea levels by the end of the century, a new study saysByAlex BrianClimate and Science reporterSome of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.Satellites give a clearer pictureIn the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days."[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More of Alexandria could be exposed to flooding than previously thought, the research saysThe ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.Sinking caused by local activitiesThe man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.Why are some cities sinking?Hear from those trying to solve the problemMethods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops."Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

schema.headline: Satellite imagery shows how fast Lagos and Alexandria are sinking

title: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'
description: Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use
body: Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women". On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early". "From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans."There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure."AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."On Wednesday, an Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."On Thursday night, Frostrup completed her fourth bushtucker trial, which is voted for by the public. Many viewers defended Odudu after the encounter.They included broadcaster and comic Judi Love who said she felt "triggered by Frostrup's comment, while Britain's Got Talent judge and Strictly Come Dancing judge Motsi Mabuse also gave their support to Odudu.BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."

schema.headline: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'

title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
description: The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal doc
body: The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip. This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before."Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything. "But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.Some viewers might be left in tears, others may think it's too schmaltzy - either way, they're going to be talking about it. It packs an emotional punch, even though it's more of a self-scripted, video diary than a conventional, journalistic documentary."This will be a documentary that most people can relate to and will admire her for doing. There is an emotional directness that's an unusual departure," says royal commentator Prof Pauline MacLaran, of Royal Holloway, University of London.MacLaran thinks it will connect well with the public, who will admire Catherine's "bravery".The documentary follows Catherine's Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the biggest mountains in England, Wales and Scotland in a single day, and the cameras record her driving in between and her encounters with other climbers.This climb is a big mountainous metaphor for the difficulties, resilience and help of other people during the "scary, disorientating experience" of her treatment.At the summit of one peak she gets voice messages from her three children - George, Louis and Charlotte - who each in turn send their love in a way that shows the closeness of their family. They also all hug and kiss later, along with Prince William, with tears being brushed away.Those moments could be the emotional peaks that people will share, in a documentary made for the social media age.It's also probably the most we've heard directly from the royal children.Somewhere, the late Prince Philip will be scratching his head at how much the royals have dropped their tradition of privacy. Although we don't learn from the film the type of cancer or any details of Catherine's treatment."No previous generation of the Royal Family would have considered producing something like this," says Valentine Low, author and royal commentator."They would have been less willing to talk about illness and personal matters," he says.But this documentary is in keeping, says Low, with a generation "that's more likely to think in terms of whether there could be a positive message from the experience".Nonetheless, says Low, such a film-making approach, sharing their own chosen thoughts with the camera without an interviewer, still allows Catherine to "control the narrative".And there are questions that arise. She speaks of her cancer journey being a "pilgrimage" and the need to "spend time on our spiritual health" - and it makes you wonder whether there has been a deeply religious or spiritual experience as part of her recovery.There's a melancholy tone to the documentary, describing the impact of a "really dark time", and you wonder how this will sit alongside the expectations of her future royal life, when she will be queen.It could also raise wider questions about the treatment, waiting times and recovery support available to the great majority of NHS patients, who do not have royal titles, but whose needs are as intense.But we see Catherine in this documentary in hospital wards sharing experiences with other cancer patients and hearing about their hopes and fears. It's deliberately raw and unadorned in how it's presented.There are lighter moments too, joking with her brother James as they head up the mountains.Speaking at a screening, Catherine said the documentary was about "giving back" to people facing similar health worries and also to recognise the support of health services and charities working with patients and families.Proceeds from the documentary, like her Three Peaks Challenge fundraiser, will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, in support of the hospital where she received treatment.The open, empathetic tone of the documentary has been warmly welcomed by those working with cancer patients."Watching someone speak so openly about the fear, the hope and the long road to recovery can make a real difference to those going through it," says Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK."Her honesty will help many people feel less alone, and it will encourage important conversations about cancer in homes across the country."Ceinwen Giles, co-chief executive of Shine Cancer Support, said: "The film's honesty is what makes it so powerful. "By being open about her experience, the princess gives others a way to start their own conversations about how cancer affects every part of a person's life, particularly younger adults and those with young families."Catherine herself says that her experience has made her think about well-being in a much more holistic way, "not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live.""My hope is that this film will encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times," she says.Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

schema.headline: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip

title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
description: If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took
body: If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism. Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power."Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people". He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. "These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship. "So, I believe that young must mobilise."As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

schema.headline: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes

title: Charity set up in Captain Sir Tom Moore's name bids to be struck off
description: A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.The charity is now known as the 1189808
body: A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Sir Tom's name at the request of his family last year.An application to have it struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.The World War Two veteran became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising £39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire.However, the charity founded in his name became mired in controversy after the charities watchdog found misconduct and mismanagement on the part of his daughter and her husband in their running of it.The Charity Commission's report uncovered a "repeated pattern of behaviour" through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling "misled".A £1.4m book deal and an £18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores were found to have enjoyed through the Captain Tom Foundation.They have already been banned from being charity trustees and earlier resigned from the foundation.The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.The father-of-two died aged 100 in February 2021 with coronavirus.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.

title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing numberByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondentReporting fromRiyadhTen days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh."I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/ReutersImage caption, Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 OctoberHaving been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic."Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month. Image source, Saudi Press Agency/ReutersImage caption, Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land. The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though. Image source, BBC/Liam WeirImage caption, Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normalRestaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.Image source, BBC/Liam WeirImage caption, Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal withBritish expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school."There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 NovemberThe fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

schema.headline: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security

title: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings
description: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home
body: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day."I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that."So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past. "You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train. Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared. He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face. The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape. "I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others. Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

schema.headline: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings

title: NHS Grampian publishes leaked report at centre of hospital scandal
description: Image caption, Lawyer Aamer Anwar is representing whistleblower Dr Mohammed Habib, who leaked the 2022 reportByKaty ScottBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours a
body: Image caption, Lawyer Aamer Anwar is representing whistleblower Dr Mohammed Habib, who leaked the 2022 reportByKaty ScottBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoNHS Grampian has published the internal report which revealed there had been 19 avoidable deaths of patients who had undergone liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.It was leaked last week by surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide probe after the report said some patients bled to death on the operating table.NHS Grampian has now released the report from September 2022, along with a redacted version of a follow-up from November the same year.The health board said they were being published, external now "in the interests of absolute transparency".Meanwhile, written submissions have also been published from witnesses who will appear at the Scottish Parliament's health committee next week.These include two whistleblowers and Prof Caroline Hiscox, former chief executive NHS Grampian.Confidential papers foundSeparately, the health board has apologised after confidential papers containing sensitive medical and personal details of 22 patients were found discarded on a street near Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.A passer-by found the documents near a bin on Raeden Park Road, near Foresterhill Health Campus, on Thursday.NHS Grampian has been at the centre of controversy since a report from the health watchdog published two weeks ago highlighted "major deficiencies" in its leadership and culture.Habib, a consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), leaked the 2022 report the following week.The Scottish government then announced an independent review into concerns around hepatobiliary (HPB) surgery at the health board.A number of patients have come forward to raise concerns about their treatment.On Thursday, Scotland's chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith, who had faced questions over his role, resigned on mental health grounds. The September 2022 report was written by Prof Stephen Wigmore, regius professor of clinical surgery at Edinburgh University.It looked at 45 patients in the care of liver and pancreatic services at ARI between 2015 and 2021.It said 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.The review criticised decision-making in liver surgery for occasionally being "overly aggressive", with surgery going ahead even if the disease was thought to be inoperable.In pancreatic surgery, patients were regularly rushed into theatre without adequate planning or consideration of non-surgical alternatives, the report said.Image caption, Laura Skaife-Knight urged anyone with concerns about their care to contact the health boardA follow-up report was published in November 2022 where Wigmore was asked to review more HPB surgery cases which had not been within the scope of his original report.It found unacceptably high mortality rates for some pancreatic surgeries, as well as "extremely high" blood loss for a number of pancreas and liver operations.The professor said surgeons had low caseloads, which harmed their technical experience.He offered to support the surgeons, then issued a letter in May 2023 which said  HPB services at NHS Grampian had improved and was now safe.Psychological support The health board's chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight said that following the presentation of the Wigmore report in 2022, there had been Serious Adverse Event Reviews (SAERs) for patients where the circumstances surrounding their deaths warranted detailed investigation."These reviews included the offer of engagement with and psychological support for affected families," she said."We have welcomed the independent review into HPB at NHS Grampian and it's important we don't pre-empt the findings of this work. We will co-operate fulsomely and in a way that is nothing other than open and honest."She said the names of patients and families had been redacted from the second report to protect their identities, and the health board was "contacting/re-engaging" them to offer support."I recognise the significant concern the events of the last week have caused our patients and local community," she said."However, I would encourage anyone who needs our care to come forward at the earliest opportunity. "Please continue to engage with our healthcare services and attend appointments and operations as normal. Our priority remains patient safety."Prof Hiscox, who was in charge of NHS Grampian when the reports were written,  has submitted evidence ahead of the Holyrood health committee meeting on Wednesday.She said the NHS Grampian board was fully briefed on the first Wigmore report at a meeting on 27 October 2022.This was done to "protect patient and staff confidentiality", provide time for patients and families to be contacted, and "enable full and frank discussion of the issues and avoid causing undue public alarm that could potentially increase the likelihood of late presentation and possibly lead to poorer health outcomes".Her evidence said this "communications approach was shared with relevant officials at Scottish government".She also said the families of 17 of the 19 patients whose deaths had been avoidable were contacted, but contact details could not be identified for the other two.A Scottish government spokesperson said the documents released to date had shown that a number of government officials were aware of the concerns raised by Dr Habib."It is a matter of public record that the Scottish government has engaged on the concerns raised by Dr Habib over a number of years," it said.The spokesperson added that the independent review would deliver "clarity, transparency and accountability to patients and their families".The committee will also hear from two whistleblowers who have raised concerns about patient safety at NHS Grampian.In his evidence ahead of the hearing, Dr Izhar Khan - who currently works as a consultant pephrologist at ARI - said the roots of the problems dated back more than 14 years."For years senior management has not listened to clinical advice and on occasions when advice was given, often it was ignored," he said.The senior clinician also said he believed Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, Moray, was not fit for purpose to deliver acute services.Dr Khan said the health board needed "strong and resilient leadership that listens to clinicians and staff".Prof Zygmunt Krukowski, former consultant general surgeon at ARI, has also written to the committee ahead of his appearance.He said it was "distressing" to see the reputation of the hospital where he worked for more than 40 years damaged by "inept management and clinical governance"."If there had been effective clinical leadership and management the pattern of poor care which was clinically obvious as early as 2010 would have been addressed," he added.Discarded documents investigationThe confidential papers found discarded on a street on Thursday are believed to consist of four crumpled pages, dated from the day before.They are understood to have listed names, CHI numbers and medical conditions of 22 neurosurgery patients.NHS Grampian's senior information risk officer, Shantini Paranjothy said: "We are making efforts to contact those patients whose data was contained in these documents and apologise for the distress this has caused."Investigations into how these documents ended up in a public place are under way and this incident has been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office."Patients have the right to expect their data to be stored securely. We take the issue of data protection very seriously."

schema.headline: NHS Grampian publishes leaked report at centre of hospital scandal

title: Why snooker could be the most mentally challenging sport
description: Figure caption, The unique psychological challenges of elite level snookerByJoe LynskeyBBC Sport senior journalistIt is perhaps one of the most viscer
body: Figure caption, The unique psychological challenges of elite level snookerByJoe LynskeyBBC Sport senior journalistIt is perhaps one of the most visceral and deeply human interviews that any sportsperson has ever given.When Mark Allen, snooker's world number 11, spoke live on TNT Sports, external in October, he said he was in a "bad place", that he didn't see a future in the game, and that he was "just trying to survive".Allen had just been beaten at the Northern Ireland Open. It was his first match since the World Championship, when in May he was one black ball away from a place in the final.He has not spoken publicly since. In a post on social media in early November, Allen said the future is "looking brighter",, external although this week he explained he was having a "very tough" time, external and was "definitely stuck in a major low right now".While Allen has not publicly discussed the reasons for his struggles, and if it is related to the sport, he had previously said "there is more to life than just a career". And this would be far from the first time that poor mental health has affected a snooker player.Right from the 1970s and the sport's first television boom, some of its great characters have spoken openly, and regularly, about addiction, isolation and snooker's unique psychological challenges.So what is it about the sport that makes it so mentally difficult? And what is being done to help?If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this story you can visit BBC Action Line, which has details of a range of advice and support.Why is snooker so 'mentally destructive'?In his emotional interview, Allen said he had spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself to play in Belfast, though he planned to continue his treatment.Other players have also previously spoken candidly about their own struggles, including multiple world champions Ronnie O'Sullivan and Mark Selby.Selby considered retirement after a first-round defeat at the 2024 World Championship, while in 2025 O'Sullivan said many players "suffer in silence".Snooker is, perhaps alongside golf, one of the most intensely individual sports, where players spend long hours alone in dimly lit practice rooms or travelling on the road, and where entire livelihoods can come down to tiny misjudgements."At least in golf you have your own ball. You don't have to worry about anyone else," 1997 world champion Ken Doherty told BBC Sport."In snooker, when you're sitting in your chair and your opponent is at the table, you can do nothing. Only sit and bear it."That is the toughest part about our sport and mentally that is quite difficult for people to comprehend."Dr Paul Gaffney is a psychologist who has worked with Allen for the past four seasons. Snooker players, he says, can feel like they are inside a "colosseum". "There are people looking down at you, and you can absolutely thrive, or be beaten in front of the world stage."Gary Wilson, the world number 28, has also spoken openly about the bouts of depression he has suffered during his 22-year career."It's a very lonely sport," the 41-year-old told BBC Sport."You're practising in a club and you could be in there on your own for six, seven, eight hours a day in a dark room, with just a snooker light on."It can get unhealthy mentally in itself, but it's what you've got to do. You've got to dedicate yourself to it."I think it is a more mentally destructive sport, potentially, than a lot of other individual sports."When asked how he felt watching Allen's interview, Wilson said: "We can all relate."There are a lot of lads who are a lot lower down on the tour struggling."Every couple of years, this coming out and nothing being done about it, isn't really good enough."Figure caption, Emotional Allen tells the BBC he is contemplating retirement following NI Open exitWhat is being done to help - and is it enough?Since 2021, snooker's governing body, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA), has put mental health provisions in place for players in the form of a partnership with Sporting Chance, a charity founded by former Arsenal and England footballer Tony Adams.In the five years since the partnership was formed, Sporting Chance has provided more than 180 sessions of counselling for a wide range of issues.Players experiencing mental health issues are encouraged to ring a confidential 24/7 helpline, and Sporting Chance will then arrange free treatment with a qualified therapist. This can take place over six to 12 talking sessions.But some players believe that support could go further. In an interview in January 2025, O'Sullivan and Selby said they would like to see mental health professionals operate on-site at tournaments."I think players would have a lot more inclination to use somebody physically there at tournaments. I don't know how feasible that is," said Wilson.There are benefits and drawbacks to the Sporting Chance service. Players receive a bespoke counsellor, rather than one who may speak to every player, but they are required to reach out themselves for this through a helpline. Doherty, who sits on the WPBSA players' board, believes it is the best solution."Players don't necessarily want to go and speak to someone at a tournament," Doherty said."We thought about having someone on hand, but then we thought, we don't think anyone would use it."This is a free service. Nobody has to know. Nobody will know on the circuit. It's just you and the person you're talking to."I know Ronnie [O'Sullivan] and Mark [Selby] spoke about that, but they obviously didn't know that service was there for them, that it's free, and that it's available for the whole tour."WPBSA chairman Jason Ferguson, a former professional player himself, said: "The highs are very high and the lows are very low."If there's anything we can work on, it's continually getting the message out to other players to say those services are there."Figure caption, How Tony Adams' charity is helping snooker players - but could more be done?In 2021, Wilson said he felt "totally gone" when the depression he explained he was suffering with came to a head in a match against John Higgins.Wilson missed a pot, and while still down on his shot, thrashed the cue ball into a neighbouring red,, external sending the frame into chaos. He was fined £250 and received a formal warning.But Wilson - known as the Tyneside Terror - believes there could be a more liberal approach to such displays of emotion in this most gentlemanly of sports."You're expected to keep your emotions completely in check at all times," he said."Now that's just not sport. When you look at any other sport that you play… you've got to be able to vent."In response, Ferguson said that while snooker's authorities and fans love to see such passion, fundamentally it is a sport of "great etiquette".Allen is next due to play in the UK Championship - a tournament he won in 2022 - which starts on Saturday. He has been drawn against qualifier Yuan Sijun but has not spoken publicly about whether he will play.For Dr Gaffney, watching Allen's interview at Belfast's Waterfront venue was "painful". It made him feel "sadness, but also admiration"."The brilliant thing about what he's done - his courage, his integrity, his class in the last few weeks - is there will be people watching snooker who wouldn't have been watching snooker before, because Mark Allen is playing," said Dr Gaffney, "and I think that says everything about the man."

schema.headline: Why snooker could be the most mentally challenging sport

title: Nations Championship: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale
description: Figure caption, Highlights: Ireland 38-14 AustraliaByJonathan BradleyBBC Sport NI senior journalistNations ChampionshipIreland (17) 38Tries: Henshaw,
body: Figure caption, Highlights: Ireland 38-14 AustraliaByJonathan BradleyBBC Sport NI senior journalistNations ChampionshipIreland (17) 38Tries: Henshaw, Timoney, Baloucoune, McNabney 2 Cons: Prendergast 5 Pen: PrendergastAustralia (7) 14Tries: Williams, Thomas Cons: Gordon 2 Ireland secured a fifth-place finish in the inaugural Nations Championship thanks to a 38-14 victory over Australia in London.While last week's 20-17 win over South Africa was the undoubted highlight of their campaign, victory on Friday night ensured Ireland won all four games they played in November.After Italy narrowly beat Fiji in the first game of the day, Ireland started slowly in a sparsely populated Allianz Stadium with the Wallabies taking a deserved lead through Jeremy Williams' try. Andy Farrell's side took control of the contest through 24 unanswered points either side of half-time with Robbie Henshaw, Nick Timoney and Robert Baloucoune crossing for scores, while Sam Prendergast converted all three and added a penalty. Kalani Thomas briefly stalled Ireland's momentum, but replacement back row James McNabney marked his second cap with a pair of tries in the final seven minutes to give the number two side in the world a comfortable, if not always convincing, victory.After what was their final Test match of 2026, Ireland finish the year with a record of 10 wins and two losses from 12 internationals. After making only two forced changes from the side who beat the Springboks six days ago - the banned Dan Sheehan and ill Mack Hansen the ones to miss out - head coach Farrell had called on his squad to back up their performance against the reigning world champions.The early stages, however, had none of the tempo or accuracy from last week in the Aviva Stadium. Sloppy knock-ons, coupled with a pair of scrum penalties, saw Ireland struggle to gain a foothold in the contest.For all Australia's territory and possession, the Wallabies took until the 23rd minute to press home their advantage on the scoreboard.Previously undone by a couple of kicking errors, Les Kiss' side looked most dangerous when keeping the ball tight and it was lock Williams who burrowed over for the game's opening score.Australia's deserved lead, however, lasted just three minutes. A midfield penalty allowed Prendergast to kick for the corner and give Ireland their first visit to the opposition 22.After a sharp attack down the short side was thwarted before the line, Ireland came back inside and Stuart McCloskey spun out of a tackle well to put his centre partner Henshaw over for the try.Three minutes before the break, again aided by an Australia penalty, Ireland doubled their lead. Tadhg Beirne did well to gather a line-out with one hand and, with Ireland's centres joining the maul, number eight Timoney broke off the base for the simple score.Prendergast converted both scores and added a penalty with the last kick of the half to put Ireland in a commanding 10-point lead at the break despite their shaky start.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ireland finished the autumn with four wins from four games playedIf Ireland started slowly in the first half, they flew from the traps after the restart. Jacob Stockdale had already almost executed a fine chip-and-chase reminiscent of his best days in the green jersey before his Ulster team-mate Baloucoune scored Ireland's third in the 43rd minute.Baloucoune, 29, gathered Prendergast's measured cross-field kick over the head of James Ramm to score his fifth try of the autumn.  Australia threw everything at getting back into the game but a penalty for coming in at the side, which halted a 19-phase attack under the posts, summed up a frustrating evening with ball in hand for next year's World Cup hosts. Scrum-half Thomas did score his first international try to reduce Ireland's lead to 24-14 with 25 minutes to go, but a comeback never felt likely from an Australia side who used Kurtley Beale from the bench for the utility back's first cap in five years. While the game lost further shape in the final quarter with the arrival of a glut of replacements, Ulster's McNabney caught the eye in a short cameo.Having had his debut against Fiji cut short by a head injury two weeks ago, the back row was the beneficiary of a fearsome Irish scrum shortly before his first try and then finished things off with another close-range score in the final minute.Line-upsIreland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Stockdale; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne (capt), Baird, Van der Flier, Timoney.Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, McNabney, Doak, Frawley, Aki.Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Ramm; Gordon, Thomas; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Alaalatoa (co-capt), Canham, Williams, Hooper, Tizzano, Valetini.Replacements: Nasser, Bell, Tupou, Shaw, Wilson (co-capt), McReight, Wilson, Beale.Match officialsReferee: N Amashukeli (GRU)Assistant referees: C Ridley (RFU) & H Davidson (SRU)Television match official: R Kelly (NZRU)Foul play review officer: A Jackson (RFU)

schema.headline: Nations Championship: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale

title: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge
description: Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying i
body: Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock"."I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab. However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service."It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it."Suzanna McDonald, who leads the UKHSA's flu programme, said the H1N1 strain was fueling the spread. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the strain "does seem to have picked up a few more changes that we would have expected over the season"."But the really encouraging news was that last year when we saw a drifted strain, the vaccine still worked very well," she added. Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak."The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children."It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS. The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.  As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.  This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised. Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached. Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff. A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

schema.headline: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge

title: Police look for more than 100 gig-goers to help Co-op Live investigation
description: Image caption, More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from the arena during the rapper's concertByStewart Whittingham and Rachael LazaroNorth WestUpdate
body: Image caption, More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from the arena during the rapper's concertByStewart Whittingham and Rachael LazaroNorth WestUpdated 7 hours agoPolice have said they are trying to contact more than 100 gig-goers to help their investigation after an unknown substance was released at a concert at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.Detectives believe a "small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night".More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".No arrests have been made and the substance has not yet been identified.Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We're working to identify those [robbery] suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents. "All of this work is ongoing at pace.He said there had been "similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries".Fans reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.Image source, HandoutImage caption, Fans say they were in quarantine at the Etihad sports hall for about six hoursJess Kinyata, 20, from West London, who was one of 12,000 people evacuated from the arena, said before the "gas began" his 18 carat gold chain, worth about £1,500, was stolen from him during a set by the concert's opening artist, Victony.GMP previously said there had been nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert.Harding said officers had been "working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV".He added: "There are over a hundred people at the gig that we are working to try and contact to potentially assist with our enquiries."We thank all those that have assisted us so far."We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically."Figure caption, Joey Howe said there was confusion and panic when the show stoppedNorth West Ambulance Service said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution".Those who suffered symptoms had been taken to the Etihad stadium.Some fans complained the process, which involved them changing into paper white suits and putting their clothes in a plastic bag, was "invasive" and "traumatic".Many stayed quarantined for several hours before being able to leave in the early hours of Monday.GMP said: "People's safety, and the safety of the wider community, was at the forefront of officers' minds throughout."Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Fans said the incident happened 30 to 40 minutes into the rapper's setThe substance was released at about 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.Concertgoers have described feeling "unsafe" and seeing "distressing" scenes and people "coughing up blood".Posting on Instagram, Toliver said: "My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured."The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."Co-op Live, which reopened its doors on Thursday night for a gig by American singer Phoebe Bridgers, previously said its priority remained "the safety and security of all visitors" to the venue. schema.headline: Police look for more than 100 gig-goers to help Co-op Live investigation
